doc.title: Ellen Rowe interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 2, 2024

title: Being 'contingency oriented'
summary: Rowe reflects on a therapist's phrase about women moving from contingency to contingency, and on never imagining being an accompanist like for Joni Mitchell.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: me. And yeah, one thing led to another and I ended up getting that job. And like I said, I kind of fell into it and it’s always been interesting to me because I had a therapist once who talked about the fact that many women, maybe not so much now but at least when I was growing up — were, as she put it, “contingency oriented.” We go from contingency to contingency dealing with each thing as it comes along instead of going, “I want to be Joni Mitchell’s musical director” or whatever that might be. And so I kind of look at it that way. I think I’m lucky that I had the tools to be able to step into that job and realize that it was really rewarding and challenging and fun and then one thing led to another and I got out to Michigan. But I think had I really been able to ask myself what I most wanted, you know say in college I might have been allowed to think this way, and I don’t know why I wasn’t but you know I might have said I would love to play piano for an artist I admire, like a Joni Mitchell. But I had no concept that that was possible or that such a thing was possible, and so I was just kind of going along doing what I was told to do and trying to do it as well as I could. And I think I’m lucky in that I ended up in academia and also having a chance to play and write. But I’ve always thought a lot about that contingency oriented thing that my therapist said.
That’s a good way to put it. I think I’m that way as well, like opportunities come that I hadn’t thought about doing that, but I’ll give it a try.
